articles.title: Blind Baking a Pie Crust Prevents Underbaked Issues
articles.summary: By following certain steps and techniques, bakers can ensure their pie crusts are perfectly cooked through.
articles.content: The art of baking the perfect pie is often marred by common pitfalls, including an underbaked crust that can ruin the entire dessert. Many bakers have fallen victim to these mistakes, but one solution stands out as a way to prevent this issue: blind baking. By baking the crust before adding the filling, you can ensure that it's cooked through and doesn't end up soggy or undercooked. The key is knowing when enough color has been achieved, which depends on what type of filling will be used in the pie. For certain pies, such as those with custard fillings like pumpkin pie, partially baking the crust gives it a head start so that it's cooked through before the filling sets. Blind baking is also essential for pies with no-bake fillings, where the crust needs to be fully baked before being filled with ingredients like chocolate pudding or cranberry curd. While most traditional fruit pies don't require blind baking, there are some exceptions, such as single-crust fruit pies topped with a crumble, that benefit from this technique. Some pie recipes explicitly call for blind baking, so it's essential to follow the instructions rather than making assumptions about which fillings need it. Chilling the shaped pie shell is essential before baking to prevent it from shrinking or slumping in the oven. Cold dough holds its shape better when exposed to heat, which is why this step is crucial for achieving a perfect crust. To line the shell with parchment paper, start by crumpling it and then unfolding it to help it conform to the shape of the pan. This technique ensures that the parchment fits snugly into the corners and edges of the pie plate. Once lined, fill the shell with weights or other materials to hold the dough firmly in place while baking. Pie makers can opt for ceramic weights, dried beans, rice, or stainless-steel ball bearings to keep the crust from puffing up. These alternatives can be used interchangeably, but it's worth noting that some bakers swear by specific options over others. Jesse Szewczyk and Rebecca Firkser, editors in the Test Kitchen, prefer lighter materials to prevent compressing the dough. Their experience suggests that heavy weights can limit the expansion of buttery layers, making the crust less flaky. The chilled Perfect Pie Crust dough requires about 5 minutes at room temperature to become pliable before rolling out on a lightly floured surface to a 12-inch round, approximately ⅛ inch thick. To prevent shrinkage and ensure even baking, the rolled-out dough is carefully transferred to a 9-inch diameter pie plate, preferably made of metal. Excess flour is brushed off before placing the dough into the plate, taking care not to stretch it as it's eased into the bottom and sides. A 1-inch overhang is left around the edges, which is then folded onto itself and pressed to seal. Crimping can be done at this stage if desired. The pie crust is chilled for 15 minutes before proceeding with baking. To prevent the dough from shrinking or puffing unevenly during baking, a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet is used as a base. Two sheets of crumpled parchment paper are placed on top of the pie crust and weighed down with pie weights, dried beans, or rice to keep them in place. The oven is preheated to 375°F with a rack positioned in the lower third. The pie plate is carefully set on the prepared baking sheet before placing it in the oven for about 30-35 minutes, until the edges turn golden brown and the bottom appears opaque when checked through the parchment paper. Once baked, the oven temperature is reduced to 325°F, and the parchment paper and weights are removed. The crust is returned to the oven for an additional 12-18 minutes, or until the bottom and sides are evenly golden brown all over. When it comes to following your recipe's instructions, there are some nuances to consider when it comes to docking the crust. Preparing ahead of time is always a good idea, and for blind-baked pie crusts, you can make them up to 2 days in advance. To do so, let the cooled crust cool completely, then wrap it well and store it at room temperature until ready to fill. The length of time needed for blind-baking pie crust can vary greatly depending on what's going inside. Some pies require only a partially baked crust, while others demand a shell that's deeply golden brown. While oven temperatures and different pie plates can affect the baking time, the filling is also a crucial factor in determining how much additional baking the crust will need. As such, it's essential to use the recipe's timing as a guide but keep a close eye on the color and texture of the pastry. When aiming for a pale base, the goal is usually to prevent over-browning during the extended baking time required by fruit pies. However, this thinking isn't always accurate, and some recipes, like those for single-crust varieties topped with crumble, might call for an anemic crust from the start. For these types of pies, a pale, partially baked crust should look set rather than raw, with the bottom appearing opaque and having some light golden patches. The crimped edge may already be noticeably browned, but don't assume this is always the case, fruit pies can vary greatly in their baking requirements. A partially baked crust can give certain pies an edge when it comes to cooking time. This is particularly true for custard-based fillings that require a shorter baking period than fruit-based ones. For custard pies like chess and lemon buttermilk, the goal is to develop a solid golden base layer before the filling sets. This ensures the crust doesn't end up pale or translucent by the time it's done. A well-colored crust can make all the difference in these types of pies. The bottom of the crust should be evenly golden, with no patches of pale color visible. The sides too should have taken on some color, although they may not be as dark as the rim. Overall, the shell should look like it's well on its way to being fully baked. A recipe that produces a well-baked crust is essential for achieving this result. For instance, our perfect pie crust recipe involves baking the weighted crust until the edges are golden before removing the weights and continuing until the bottom and sides are evenly browned. Not all pies require the same level of browning, however. Some need an even more substantial head start to ensure they don't end up pale or undercooked by the time the filling is done. For example, our bourbon-date pecan pie takes its crust to a dry golden finish before adding a filling that bakes for another 45–55 minutes. When it comes to no-bake fillings like pudding or curd, the crust should be baked to a darker golden brown. This gives it a toasty, burnished color that complements these types of fillings nicely. A blind-baked pie crust is essential when a filling won't return to the oven for further cooking, allowing the crust to be fully baked through in this initial stage. The goal of pre-baking the crust is not just to achieve a dark rim around the edges but also to ensure that the entire bottom and sides are evenly browned. A well-prebaked crust should exhibit a dry, crisp texture and a rich, toasted color without any signs of doughy or translucent patches. To complete the baking process after removing the pie weights, keep a close eye on the shell's browning, checking frequently towards the end to avoid overcooking. The time required for the crust to reach full browning can vary depending on the type of dough and oven temperature, potentially taking an additional 15-20 minutes or longer than expected. articles.title: Nationwide public sector strike in France sees lower turnout than previous demonstrations
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of people participated in a nationwide public sector strike across France on Tuesday, demanding pay rises amidst rising living costs.
articles.content: Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across France on Tuesday as part of a nationwide public sector strike, demanding pay rises amidst rising living costs. The protests saw participation lower than previous demonstrations, with 146,000 people demonstrating across the country, according to official figures from the interior ministry. This is significantly fewer compared to the massive turnout seen during the last unified protest day just over a week ago, when nearly 575,000 people took part. High school and university students, as well as some private sector workers, joined in the demonstrations, bringing their voices to the government's attention on issues related to cost of living. The protests were largely peaceful around the country, with 28,000 people taking to the streets in Paris, a city that saw significantly fewer protesters than during previous demonstrations. As the protests continue to sweep across France, unions estimate that over 500,000 people have participated nationwide in the demonstrations against the rising cost of living. The number includes a significant contingent of protesters in Paris, where an estimated 175,000 took to the streets. The economic strain on France's public services has become a pressing concern for many workers, who are pushing for pay increases and better working conditions. Nurses like Aurelane Thos have been at the forefront of these demands, highlighting the dire state of hospitals and schools across the country. According to Thos, "the way things are getting worse and worse across all public services" has become a major issue that resonates with many. The protests have been marked by clashes in some cities, where police have used tear gas to disperse protesters. Meanwhile, thousands more marched peacefully through the streets of Paris, their demands for improved working conditions and higher pay echoing through the city's streets. Many protesters were seen carrying signs and banners, including a small cardboard sign held by Astrid Petit, which read "Raise salaries. As the protests enter their third month, tensions remain high between unions and the government. The failure to reach an agreement with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has left many workers feeling frustrated and disillusioned with the current state of affairs. The sound of drummers in eastern Paris was a stark contrast to the frustration felt by many workers who took to the streets across France on Tuesday. Sparkly pink and purple-clad musicians accompanied their music from union vans as protesters marched through the city's streets. The festive atmosphere belied the sense of disillusionment that has been growing among those involved in the cost-of-living protests. University professor Nicolas Prevot emphasized that the demonstrations are about more than just economic concerns. It's about defending human rights first and foremost, but also protecting public services, he said, highlighting a key issue for many protesters. The situation is further complicated by the involvement of far-right groups, with some calling for an end to what they see as government inaction. In Lyon, thousands gathered behind a banner reading Enough sacrifices for working people. A 20-year-old university student who wished to remain anonymous expressed solidarity with high school students and workers. He hoped that his voice would be heard by the government but was increasingly skeptical about being taken seriously, particularly given their focus on what he saw as minor issues. The situation in Lyon has been marked by violence in recent weeks, with a building set alight last month during clashes between protesters and security forces. Overall, however, rallies have been largely peaceful, despite accusations of police brutality and fringe violence. Authorities responded to concerns about possible further unrest by deploying security forces and temporarily banning the sale of firecrackers. The government's draft budget has sparked widespread discontent among French citizens, who are calling for a general pay rise that has been denied to public servants for four consecutive years. Unions have expressed outrage over the loss of purchasing power experienced by their members since 2017, with a staggering 16 percent decrease in real income. This economic strain is not unique to France, as protests against rising living costs are being witnessed across Europe. In Belgium, thousands of students took to the streets in Brussels on Tuesday, protesting budget cuts and increased university tuition fees that threaten their future. We're here to defend our future, declared Bastien, a 19-year-old demonstrator, highlighting the government's misplaced priorities in funding new fighter jets while slashing support for culture, health, and other essential sectors. The students' rally was marked by peaceful chants of power to the students" and anti-fascist slogans, with some participants holding signs demanding more rights and less bureaucracy. The protests serve as a stark reminder that economic policies have real-life consequences for ordinary people, who are increasingly frustrated with the government's handling of their welfare. The wave of protests sweeping across Europe underscores the urgent need for policymakers to address the growing concerns about living costs and access to education.
